757.title: Different answers
757.hook: a cure, a redemption, a patience, a judgment and an open question, set side by side and not blended
757.carry: men are disturbed not by the things which happen
757.howItsDone: Some people on a spiritual path read several traditions side by side, keeping each answer in its own words, and notice which ones they return to on hard days.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was consolatio, a letter of comfort. Your line was you're not alone: one person reaching toward another, and either may end up comforted.

Five people sit at one kitchen table. Each has buried someone, or lost a job, or sat up with a fever that wouldn't break. Ask them all the same question: what do you do with suffering? One talks about a fire that can go out. One talks about a cross. One says a word that means patience. One says it depends on what you tell yourself. And the last says, honestly, I don't know, and I keep asking. It would be easy to blend those five into one soft sentence. This year promised not to.
screen: `FIVE PEOPLE, ONE TABLE.` → `FIVE DIFFERENT ANSWERS.` → `NONE BLENDED.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha. In the four noble truths, suffering has a cause, craving, and so it can cease. Buddhists call that ceasing nibbana, and some teachers picture it as a flame that goes out when the fuel is gone. The answer is a cure: see the cause, walk the path, and the burning cools. Second, the cross. Christians don't explain suffering away. They say that in Jesus, God entered it, and that it can be redeemed, taken up into something that heals. Revelation looks ahead to a day when "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes." Third, the Quran. Hardship is met with sabr, patient endurance, and with prayer: "Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast." And in a short surah, a line said twice in a row: "with hardship goeth ease." Fourth, the Stoics. Epictetus taught that much of the hurt lives in our judgment. In George Long's translation: "Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things." Change the judgment, he says, and you change much of the disturbance. Fifth, Job. The book gives no reason at all. God speaks out of a whirlwind and asks, "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?" The question stays open. A cure, a redemption, a patience, a judgment, an open question. Nobody here is asked to make them fit. Each belongs to people who have lived by it on their worst nights.
screen: `THE BUDDHA: IT CAN CEASE.` · `THE CROSS: IT CAN BE REDEEMED.` · `THE QURAN: PATIENCE, AND EASE.` · `EPICTETUS: THE JUDGMENT HURTS.` · `JOB: THE QUESTION STAYS OPEN.` · then, large: `DIFFERENT ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Let the five answers come back one at a time: it can cease; it can be redeemed; patience, and ease with hardship; the judgment is what hurts; the question stays open. Notice which you lean toward and which you lean away from, and whether one fits a small trouble and another a large one. You don't have to choose; just notice the lean.
Different answers: the traditions meet suffering with a cure, a redemption, a patience, a judgment and an open question, each in its own voice. Today's word.
Your line: men are disturbed not by the things which happen. One answer among five, kept in its own words. Until next time.

758.title: Suffering close
758.hook: weeks on a hard question, and no bow tied on it
758.howItsDone: Some people who study suffering across traditions end not with a single answer but with a way of holding pain: slowly, without forcing a lesson, and in company.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was different answers: a cure, a redemption, a patience, a judgment and an open question, kept apart. Your line was men are disturbed not by the things which happen.
screen: `MEN ARE DISTURBED NOT BY THE THINGS WHICH HAPPEN.`

segments.voice: If you kept a notebook through this block, it holds an odd collection by now. A pain named plainly. A complaint written the way the psalmists wrote theirs. The name of a far-off place. A map of what actually helps. A letter to the person you used to be. A note sent to someone hurting. None of it adds up to a solution, and that's not a failure. The honest ending to weeks on a hard question isn't a bow tied on top. It's a way of holding what's still there.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK OF ODD THINGS.` → `NO BOW ON TOP.` → `ONE WAY TO HOLD IT.`

segments.voice: First, the naming. The block began with the Buddha, who names suffering before anything else, the way a doctor names an illness, and with the second arrow, the pain we add to the pain. You can't hold what you won't look at. Second, the arguing. Job sat in the ashes, and his friends "sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." Then they started explaining, and got it wrong. The Psalms let a person argue with God: "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD?" Third, the holding. Sabr in the Quran, Krishna's counsel in the Gita to bear heat and cold, Guru Arjan finding God's will sweet, the Sikh hukam. Each, in its own words, teaches a way to stay steady inside what can't be changed. Fourth, the company. Shiva, the Jewish house of mourning, with visitors sitting beside the mourners. Less advice, more presence. A hand on the heart and the plain words: others feel this too. Help from a professional, counted as strength. Together it doesn't make a theory. It makes a manner. Not forcing a lesson out of pain. Not hurrying anyone, including yourself. Not ranking whose suffering counts. The word for that manner is the one this block ends on: gently. Tomorrow the year turns to a question right next to this one, and the same manner will be needed there too.
screen: `THE NAMING: THE PAIN AND THE ARROW.` · `THE ARGUING: JOB AND THE PSALMS.` · `THE HOLDING: STEADY INSIDE IT.` · `THE COMPANY: PRESENCE OVER ADVICE.` · then, large: `GENTLY.`

segments.voice: Sit gently; that's the whole practice. Let the body be heavy and the breath come at its own pace, and if something hard from these weeks comes back, let it sit beside you, the way Job's friends sat before they spoke. If your mind wanders, bring it back the way you'd guide a child by the hand, not the way you'd yank a leash.
Job, who sat in the ashes while his friends kept silent before they started explaining, and got it wrong. Today's word.
Your line: gently. Nothing in these weeks has to be solved first. See you tomorrow.

759.title: The oldest question
759.hook: the voices this year listens to each speak about death, and they do not agree
759.howItsDone: Some people exploring death across traditions begin by writing down what they believe now, so they can notice later what the teachers changed and what they didn't.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the block on suffering closed on Job, and one word for how to hold what's left. Your line was gently.

What happens when we die? A child asks it at bedtime, out of nowhere, with the light already off. An adult asks it at a funeral, quietly, or not at all. Call it the oldest question, though nobody can put a date on that. The voices this year listens to each have something to say about death, and they don't say the same thing. A new block begins, and before anyone else speaks, one voice goes first: yours.
screen: `A CHILD ASKS WITH THE LIGHT OFF.` → `THE VOICES DON'T AGREE.` → `YOURS GOES FIRST.`

segments.voice: First, they don't agree. In the weeks ahead, Socrates will offer two possibilities and refuse to pick. An Epicurean poet will say death is nothing to us. Buddhists will speak of rebirth without a fixed soul passing on. The Gita will speak of a self that sets down bodies like worn clothes. Christians will speak of resurrection, Muslims of a day when every deed is weighed, Confucius of attending to life first. These aren't one answer in different costumes, and this block keeps each in its own home, as the block on suffering did. Second, the Bible has a book that sits squarely in this question. Ecclesiastes says there is "a time to be born, and a time to die." It doesn't explain the second half. It sets the two side by side. Third, why start with you. Across weeks of teachers, it's easy to lose track of what you thought before they spoke. So today you write it down plainly, in a few lines: what you think happens, what you hope, what you fear, and what you honestly don't know. At the end of the block, you'll be invited to write it again and see what moved. Fourth, gently. Death is not an abstract topic for anyone grieving. If a loss is fresh, it's fine to go slowly through these weeks, or to sit a practice out. The question has waited a long time. It can wait for you.
screen: `THEY DON'T AGREE.` · `A TIME TO BE BORN, A TIME TO DIE.` · `WRITE WHAT YOU THINK BEFORE THEY SPEAK.` · `GENTLY, IF THE LOSS IS FRESH.` · then, large: `WHAT I THINK NOW.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself plainly: what do I think happens when we die? It may be the answer you were raised with or one you came to on your own; notice what comes first, a picture, a word, a shrug, a fear, a face, or I don't know, which is an answer too. Let it come and stay, as plain as a grocery list.
Ecclesiastes, the book that says there is a time to be born, and a time to die, without explaining the second half. Today's word.
Your line: what I think now. A few plain lines, dated, waiting for the end of the block. That's day seven hundred fifty-nine.

760.title: Sleep or journey
760.hook: Socrates, just sentenced to death: it is either a dreamless sleep or a journey, and neither is to be feared
760.howItsDone: Students of philosophy read Socrates's closing words in Plato's Apology as an example of facing death with reasoning rather than fear, without claiming to know what death is.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Ecclesiastes: a time to be born, and a time to die. Your line was what I think now, your own voice before the teachers'.

The vote has just been counted. An Athenian jury has sentenced an old man to death for corrupting the young and failing to honor the city's gods. A person might rage, or beg, or go silent. Socrates turns to the jurors who voted to acquit him and says, in effect: stay a minute, friends, let's talk while the officials are busy. And what he wants to talk about is the thing just handed to him. In Plato's account of the trial, the Apology, he lays out two possibilities for what death is, two doors, and walks through neither.
screen: `THE VERDICT IS IN.` → `STAY A MINUTE, FRIENDS.` → `TWO POSSIBILITIES.`

segments.voice: First, a silence he trusts. Socrates says an inner sign has all his life stopped him when he was about to do wrong, even in small things. That day it never stopped him: not leaving home, not walking into court, not in his speech. He takes its silence as a hint that what is happening may be good. Second, the first door: sleep. Maybe death is nothing at all, no awareness, like a night of sleep without even a dream. Think of your best night of deep sleep, he tells the jurors, and set it against all the other days and nights of your life. Even the great king of Persia, he says, would find few days and nights better. If death is like that, he says, it is a gain. Third, the second door: a journey. Maybe death is a move to another place, where the dead are. Then he would meet the poets and heroes of old and keep asking questions, testing who is wise. And there, he jokes, they surely don't put you to death for asking. Fourth, either way. Socrates doesn't claim to know which door is real. His point is that neither gives a reason to be afraid. He tells them a good person has nothing evil to fear, in life or after death. And he ends: now it's time to go, I to die and you to live, and which of us goes to the better thing, only God knows. That is Plato's Socrates. Others in this block will answer differently, on their own days.
screen: `THE SIGN THAT STAYED SILENT.` · `DOOR ONE: A DREAMLESS SLEEP.` · `DOOR TWO: A JOURNEY.` · `NEITHER IS TO BE FEARED.` · then, large: `EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Take the first door: think of the deepest sleep you can remember, the kind where no time seemed to pass, and rest there a few breaths. Then take the second: a long trip, a new place, people you've wanted to meet, and rest there too. Hold both without choosing, and notice whether fear shows up in either; if this is tender today, rest in the breath instead.
Hypnos, Socrates's first picture of death in Plato's Apology: a sleep with no dream, no cause for fear. Today's word.
Your line: either way. Two doors, and fear behind neither. Day seven hundred sixty, done.

761.title: Practicing dying
761.hook: in the Phaedo, Socrates calls philosophy a practice of dying, and his friend laughs
761.howItsDone: Readers of the Phaedo take 'practicing dying' in different ways: as Plato's argument that the soul is freed from the body, or more loosely as a daily habit of small lettings go.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hypnos, Socrates's dreamless sleep. Your line was either way: sleep or journey, and fear in neither.

A prison cell in Athens, on the last day. Socrates's friends have come early. His wife and small son have been with him and been sent home. The talk turns to philosophy, and Socrates says something so strange that his friend Simmias laughs out loud: people who do philosophy rightly are doing nothing other than practicing dying. The crowd would agree, Simmias says, still laughing: philosophers do seem half dead already. Socrates doesn't mind the joke. He means something else.
screen: `A CELL ON THE LAST DAY.` → `SIMMIAS LAUGHS.` → `PRACTICE DYING?`

segments.voice: First, the claim. In Plato's dialogue the Phaedo, Socrates says those who truly love wisdom are practicing dying and being dead, so of all people they should be least afraid when death actually comes. Someone who trains all their life for something shouldn't panic when it arrives. Second, what he means by dying. For Plato's Socrates, death is the soul's release from the body, and philosophy is a rehearsal of that release. Each time the mind lets go of the body's pulls, hunger and craving, fear and display, the restless wanting more, it steps back from them a little. Philosophy, in his sense, is that stepping back, practiced daily. Third, the honest limit. This picture rests on a belief: that the soul is separate from the body and can go on without it. Much of the Phaedo argues for that belief. Not everyone in this block shares it; tomorrow's teacher, for one, does not. That disagreement is real, and it stays standing. Fourth, what can travel. Some readers who don't share Plato's view of the soul still keep the practice. They hear it as this: every small letting go, a grudge set down, a habit loosened, a possession given away, an argument you don't need to win, is a rehearsal for the larger letting go that comes to everyone. Practiced small and often, it stops being foreign.
screen: `THOSE WHO LOVE WISDOM PRACTICE DYING.` · `STEPPING BACK FROM THE BODY'S PULLS.` · `IT RESTS ON PLATO'S SOUL.` · `SMALL LETTINGS GO, PRACTICED OFTEN.` · then, large: `PRACTICE LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small thing you're holding tightly today: a plan that has to go a certain way, a comment you're still chewing on, a phone you keep reaching for. Notice where the holding sits, a jaw, a hand, a chest, and on each out-breath loosen that spot a little, the way you'd open a fist one finger at a time. You don't have to throw the thing away; just hold it with an open hand.
Practicing dying: in Plato's Phaedo, philosophy as a daily rehearsal of letting go, so that the last letting go is not a stranger. Today's word.
Your line: practice letting go. Simmias laughed, but Socrates meant every word of it. See you tomorrow.

762.title: The time before
762.hook: Lucretius: the ages before we were born didn't trouble us, and the ages after won't either
762.carry: a mirror of the time to come
762.howItsDone: Some readers of Lucretius use his mirror as a reflection: they recall the long time before their birth and set it beside the time after death, to see whether the fear changes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in a prison cell, Socrates called philosophy a practice of dying. Your line was practice letting go.

Somewhere there's a photograph of your parents, or grandparents, from before you were born. A wedding, a beach, a kitchen with ugly wallpaper. They're laughing at something. The light is the same light. The world is busy and complete, and you are nowhere in it. Is there anything painful in being absent from it? A Roman poet named Lucretius asked a question very like that, and built a whole argument about death on the answer.
screen: `A PHOTO FROM BEFORE YOU.` → `ANYTHING PAINFUL IN THAT?` → `A POET BUILDS ON IT.`

segments.voice: First, the poet. Lucretius wrote a long poem in Latin verse, On the Nature of Things, to explain the teaching of the Greek philosopher Epicurus. In that teaching everything, the soul included, is made of tiny particles, and at death they scatter. No one is left to suffer anything. In the third book he says it in a single line: death is nothing to us. Second, the history lesson. He recalls a terrible time, when Carthage came against Rome from every side and the whole world shook, unsure who would rule land and sea. And we, he says, felt nothing. We weren't there yet. So when we are no longer here, nothing can touch us, not even if earth and sea and sky are thrown together. Third, the mirror. Look back, he says, at the endless ages that passed before we were born. Nature holds that time up to us like a mirror of the time to come after we die. Is there anything frightful in it? Anything gloomy? Isn't it more peaceful than any sleep? Fourth, the honest reply. Not every reader is persuaded. Some answer that what they fear isn't being dead; it's losing this: the people, the morning light, the unfinished things. The mirror doesn't speak to that, and other voices in this block reject Lucretius's view of the soul. But the picture still makes the vast stretch of nothing before you feel familiar, even restful.
screen: `DEATH IS NOTHING TO US.` · `WHEN CARTHAGE CAME, WE FELT NOTHING.` · `THE TIME BEFORE IS A MIRROR.` · `NOT EVERY READER IS PERSUADED.` · then, large: `THE TIME BEFORE.`

segments.voice: Picture a moment from before you were born, a grandparent as a child, a street years before you walked it, a storm nobody remembers now, vivid with weather and sound and people busy with their lives. Notice that you're absent from it, and how that absence feels, calm, strange, or nothing at all, without pushing toward any conclusion. If the time after comes in, let it sit beside the time before, two quiet rooms.
Lucretius, the Roman poet who held up the ages before our birth as a mirror for the time after death. Today's word.

763.title: To learn to die
763.hook: Montaigne: to philosophize is to learn to die, and he'd like death to find him planting cabbages
763.howItsDone: Some readers of Montaigne take his essay as an invitation to think about death calmly and often, not to dwell on it, but to loosen the fear and get on with ordinary life.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Lucretius, whose mirror is the time before we were born. Your line was a mirror of the time to come.
screen: `A MIRROR OF THE TIME TO COME.`

segments.voice: A man sits at a writing table in France, working on short pieces that wander from quotation to gossip to confession and back. He is not a priest or a professor. He is a reader who wants to know how to live. One piece takes its title from a line of Cicero's: that to philosophize is to learn to die. Michel de Montaigne writes it plainly, and somewhere in it he says how he would like death to find him. Not in some grand last scene. Planting cabbages.
screen: `A MAN AT A WRITING TABLE.` → `AN OLD ROMAN SAYING.` → `PLANTING CABBAGES.`

segments.voice: First, the title. Montaigne opens by citing Cicero: to philosophize is nothing other than to prepare for death. He takes the line seriously, then makes it his own. Second, the usual remedy, and his complaint. Ordinary people, he says, deal with death by not thinking about it, and he calls that a kind of blindness: when it comes, to them or to someone they love, it lands with full force on someone unprepared. His answer: take away death's strangeness. Spend time with it. Get used to it. Keep it in mind often, not to be gloomy, but so it stops being a stranger at the door. Third, why bother. To think ahead about death, he says, is to think ahead about freedom: a person who has learned how to die has unlearned how to be a slave. Knowing how to die, he goes on, frees us from every kind of subjection and constraint. Loosen that one fear, and much else loosens. Fourth, the cabbages. Here's the turn. He doesn't want to spend his life brooding. He wants to be busy with ordinary work, and he'd like death to find him planting his cabbages, not caring about death, and caring even less about the garden left unfinished. That's the week, too: five answers to suffering kept apart, Socrates's either way, Plato's practice of letting go, Lucretius's mirror, and now Montaigne, learning to die so that he can go on planting.
screen: `TO PHILOSOPHIZE IS TO PREPARE FOR DEATH.` · `TAKE AWAY ITS STRANGENESS.` · `LEARN TO DIE, UNLEARN BEING A SLAVE.` · `FOUND PLANTING CABBAGES.` · then, large: `LEARN TO DIE.`

segments.voice: This one is gentle, and you can skip it; if a loss is close right now, rest in the breath instead. If you'd like, picture once, calmly, the plain fact that a day will come, no accident, no hospital drama, and hold it for a few breaths, the way you'd look at a stranger's face until it looks less strange. Then let it go, and see yourself doing something ordinary that you love: your own cabbages.
